questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Discuss Trilobites on the basis of the following:

(i) Diagnostic morphological features; (4 marks)

(ii) Geological history; (4 marks)

(iii) Palaeontological significance. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Diagnostic morphological features (4 marks).**

Trilobites are extinct marine arthropods (phylum Arthropoda, class Trilobita). Their diagnostic features are:

1. **Hard dorsal exoskeleton** of chitin strengthened with calcium carbonate (calcite), which is why it fossilises well; the underside and the limbs are rarely preserved.
2. **Trilobed body.** Two longitudinal furrows divide the body into a central **axial lobe** and two side **pleural lobes**. This gives the group its name.
3. **Three transverse divisions (tagmata):** the **cephalon** (head shield), the **thorax** (a series of free, articulated segments) and the **pygidium** (tail shield made of fused segments).
4. **Cephalon structures:** a raised central **glabella** (the stomach region), cheeks (fixigenae and librigenae) separated by **facial sutures** along which the animal split open when it moulted, **compound eyes** on the free cheeks (some blind forms), and often **genal spines**.
5. **Segmented, bilaterally symmetrical body**; the articulated thorax allowed the animal to **enrol** like a woodlouse for protection. Each segment bore a pair of biramous (two-branched) limbs.
6. Most trilobites are about 1 to 10 cm long, and the **moulting (ecdysis)** of the exoskeleton produced many fossil fragments from one animal.

**(ii) Geological history (4 marks).**

- **First appearance:** the Early Cambrian (about 520 Ma); they are among the first animals with a hard skeleton and were part of the Cambrian explosion of life.
- **Rise:** they diversified rapidly in the Cambrian, when they were the dominant marine animals, and stayed abundant in the Ordovician.
- **Decline:** the group suffered extinction events at the end of the Cambrian and the Ordovician, and again in the Late Devonian, after which only one order (Proetida) survived.
- **Extinction:** the last trilobites disappeared at the **end of the Permian (about 252 Ma)** in the greatest mass extinction. They lived only in the sea (shallow shelf seas, as bottom-dwellers, swimmers and a few floaters), so their whole range is **Cambrian to Permian (Palaeozoic)**.

**(iii) Palaeontological significance (4 marks).**

1. **Index (zone) fossils** for the Cambrian and Ordovician: they evolved quickly, were abundant, were widespread and are easily preserved, so they are used for **biostratigraphic dating and correlation** of strata.
2. **Palaeoenvironment indicators:** they show shallow, normal-salinity marine conditions; the presence or absence of eyes and the type of body form suggest the depth and the way of life (burrowing, crawling, swimming).
3. **Palaeogeography:** the distribution of trilobite faunas across continents helps to reconstruct the position of old continents and oceans (support for continental drift).
4. **Evolution studies:** they give a very good record of evolutionary change (many species, growth stages and moulting), and they are among the oldest records of eyes (compound, calcite lenses).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Distinguish between the following:

(i) Chronostratigraphy and biostratigraphy; (3 marks)

(ii) Diachronous bed and marker bed; (3 marks)

(iii) Cyclic sedimentation and rhythmic sedimentation; (4 marks)

(iv) Relative dating and absolute dating. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Chronostratigraphy and biostratigraphy (3 marks).**

- **Chronostratigraphy** classifies rock strata into units according to the **time** at which they formed (eonothem, erathem, system, series, stage). These time-rock units are bounded by surfaces of the same age and are worldwide.
- **Biostratigraphy** classifies strata into units (biozones) according to their **fossil content** (range, assemblage or abundance of fossils). Biozone boundaries may cut across time lines, but biostratigraphy is the main tool used to date and correlate and so to build the chronostratigraphic scale.

**(ii) Diachronous bed and marker bed (3 marks).**

- A **diachronous bed** is a rock unit whose age is **different from place to place**; its boundaries are not time lines. Example: a transgressive beach sandstone that is deposited progressively younger inland as the shoreline advances.
- A **marker bed** (key bed) is a thin, distinctive, widely spread bed deposited **at one time (isochronous)** that can be recognised easily over a large area, for example a volcanic ash (tuff) band, a coal seam or a thin distinctive limestone. It is used for **correlation** between sections.

**(iii) Cyclic sedimentation and rhythmic sedimentation (4 marks).**

- **Cyclic sedimentation:** a succession of **three or more different rock types repeated again and again in the same order** (A-B-C, A-B-C...), for example a coal-measure cyclothem of sandstone, shale, seatearth, coal and marine band. It is caused by repeated changes such as delta switching, transgression and regression, sea-level change or tectonic movement; the order of the beds reflects a changing environment.
- **Rhythmic sedimentation:** a **regular alternation of two rock types** of similar thickness (A-B-A-B), for example alternating limestone and shale, or annual varves in a glacial lake. It is controlled by regular periodic changes such as seasons or climatic cycles, and the environment returns to the same state each time.

**(iv) Relative dating and absolute dating (3 marks).**

- **Relative dating** gives only the **order** of events or rocks (older or younger), without a number of years. Methods: the law of superposition, cross-cutting relationships, included fragments, unconformities and fossil succession.
- **Absolute dating** gives the **age in years** (numerical age). Methods: radiometric dating using the decay of radioactive isotopes (U-Pb, K-Ar, Rb-Sr, carbon-14), and also varves, tree rings and fission tracks.
